directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since Giant Poha Berry needs a long season to reach its notably larger fruit size compared to standard cape gooseberry. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, spacing plants generously to accommodate their sprawling, half-woody habit, and stake or cage the sturdy branches to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. This selection, popularized in Hawaii, produces papery husks enclosing golden-orange berries roughly twice the diameter of the wild-type poha berry, with a rich, tropical sweet-tart flavor prized fresh, dried, or cooked into jams and sauces. In zones 9-11 plants can persist as short-lived perennials and will self-seed readily in warm garden soil.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

common_name: Dixter Flame Crocosmia (Christopher Lloyd's Fiery Orange-Red Montbretia)
directions: This selection was raised at Great Dixter and carries the arching, pleated sword-like foliage typical of Crocosmia masoniorum, topped in mid to late summer by broad sprays of fiery orange-red flowers held above the leaves rather than nodding beneath them. Plant corms 3 to 4 inches deep in spring once the soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil that does not dry out completely during the growing season. Clumps bulk up quickly and benefit from division every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering. In zones colder than 6, mulch heavily over winter or lift corms in fall where hard freezes are expected.

common_name: Zizanie Gladiolus (Cream and Wine-Purple Bicolor Gladiolus)
directions: Zizanie is a widely grown large-flowered gladiolus prized for its creamy-yellow petals splashed with a bold, wine-purple blotch at the throat, a striking contrast that makes it a favorite among cut-flower growers and flower arrangers. Plant corms 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun after the last frost, and stagger plantings every two weeks through early summer to extend the bloom season. Stake tall spikes or plant in tight blocks so neighboring stems support one another against wind. Where winters drop below zone 8, lift corms after the foliage yellows in fall and store them cool and dry until spring.

common_name: Prins Claus Gladiolus (White with Raspberry-Red Blotch Gladiolus)
directions: Prins Claus produces snow-white ruffled florets marked with a vivid raspberry-red feathered blotch on the lower petals, giving each spike a crisp, high-contrast look popular in Dutch-bred gladiolus lines. Set corms 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil once danger of frost has passed, and water deeply during active growth and flowering. Deadhead spent florets from the bottom of the spike upward to keep plants tidy and redirect energy into the corm. In regions colder than zone 8, dig and store corms indoors over winter after the first light frost blackens the foliage.

Nymph is an old Dutch heirloom miniature gladiolus, bearing dainty white blooms flushed with soft pink and marked with a creamy throat blotch on wiry, weather-resistant stems well below the height of the large-flowered hybrids. Because Gladiolus nanus types are hardier than grandiflorus glads, corms can go into the ground two to three weeks before the last frost in most zones and, with a thick winter mulch, may survive outdoors down to zone 5. Plant corms 3 to 4 inches deep in full sun and well-drained soil, and mass several corms together for the best display since individual spikes are slender. Leave foliage intact after bloom to recharge the corm for next season's flowers.

Green Isle carries the same unusual chartreuse-green coloring that makes a handful of specialty gladiolus cultivars sought after by florists looking for an unconventional accent among warmer bouquet tones. Plant corms 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, spacing them in blocks rather than single rows to better support the flowering spikes. Provide consistent moisture through bud formation and bloom, then taper off once flowering finishes. In zones below 8, lift and cure corms in fall for indoor winter storage and replant the following spring.
